params.question: A body is recovered from a high-altitude trekking trail in January with a recorded core temperature of 26°C. Which post-mortem finding would most reliably help the forensic physician confirm death due to systemic hypothermia?

answers.text: Bright cherry-pink colour of livor mortis in dependent areas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cherry-pink lividity can occur in hypothermia but is also classically associated with carbon monoxide poisoning, making it an unreliable standalone indicator for confirming hypothermia.

answers.text: Wischnewski spots — reddish-brown haemorrhagic erosions in the gastric mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wischnewski spots are the most characteristic PM finding in hypothermia deaths. They result from stress-induced mucosal ischaemia and are found predominantly in the gastric fundus.

answers.text: Congestion and oedema of the lungs with frothy fluid in the airways

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulmonary oedema with frothy fluid is a non-specific finding seen in drowning, heart failure, and poisoning — it cannot confirm hypothermia specifically.

answers.text: Tardieu spots (petechial haemorrhages) on the pleural surfaces

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tardieu spots are classically associated with asphyxial deaths, not hypothermia. Their presence would raise suspicion of mechanical asphyxia rather than cold exposure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Not quite. Wischnewski spots — reddish-brown haemorrhagic erosions of the gastric mucosa, particularly the fundus — are the most reliable PM indicator of hypothermia death.
Correct! Wischnewski spots in the gastric fundus are the hallmark PM finding in hypothermia and are critical to the forensic diagnosis of cold-related death.

interactions.label: A body is found in an open field after a thunderstorm with branching, fern-like

params.question: A body is found in an open field after a thunderstorm with branching, fern-like reddish marks on the skin surface that are not true burns. What is the correct identification of this finding?

answers.text: Joule burn — the characteristic entry wound of domestic electrocution

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Joule burns (electric marks) are localised, punched-out pale lesions with a raised red rim at the current entry point in domestic or industrial electrocution — not the branching pattern described.

answers.text: Lichtenberg figures — pathognomonic of a lightning strike

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lichtenberg figures (arborescent fern-like feathering) are pathognomonic of lightning injury. They result from electron showers along the skin surface and fade within hours of death, so early PM examination is essential.

answers.text: Post-mortem skin marbling due to early decomposition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Post-mortem marbling produces a reticular (net-like) pattern following superficial veins due to haemolysis and bacterial action — it is distinct from the fern-like branching of Lichtenberg figures.

answers.text: Flash burns from an electrical arc at a nearby substation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flash burns from an electrical arc produce thermal injury to exposed skin similar to flame burns but do not create the characteristic arborescent branching pattern seen in Lichtenberg figures.

overallFeedback.feedback: The branching, fern-like marks are Lichtenberg figures, pathognomonic of lightning strike. They are not burns but surface electron tracks that fade rapidly after death — early examination is critical.

Correct! Lichtenberg figures are pathognomonic of lightning strike and must not be confused with electric marks of domestic electrocution — confusing them is a serious forensic error with medico-legal consequences.

params.question: An elderly woman is found dead at home during a cold spell. Her caretaker son claims she died peacefully in her sleep. Post-mortem reveals a core temperature of 27°C, Wischnewski spots in the gastric fundus, and no external injuries. Which medico-legal analysis is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Since there is no external trauma, the death is natural and no further investigation is warranted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Absence of external trauma does not rule out neglect or criminal liability. Hypothermia in a dependent person at home raises a duty-of-care question that must be investigated.

answers.text: The findings confirm hypothermia as the cause of death; the domestic setting and caretaker relationship necessitate investigation into possible death due to neglect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The PM findings confirm hypothermia (Wischnewski spots + low core temperature). In a dependent elderly person with a caretaker, the forensic physician must investigate whether failure of duty of care contributed to death — this is the medico-legal framework for neglect under FM2.19.

answers.text: Wischnewski spots are non-specific and insufficient to determine the cause of death with any certainty

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wischnewski spots are among the most specific PM findings for hypothermia. Combined with a core temperature of 27°C, they strongly support hypothermia as the cause of death.

answers.text: The low core temperature is a post-mortem artefact of environmental cooling and is not relevant to the cause of death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While post-mortem cooling does reduce body temperature, a core temperature of 27°C combined with Wischnewski spots establishes ante-mortem hypothermia, not merely a post-mortem artefact of ambient temperature.

overallFeedback.feedback: The PM findings (Wischnewski spots + hypothermia) in a dependent elderly person with a caretaker require investigation into possible neglect — the forensic physician must determine whether breach of duty of care contributed to death.

Correct! Hypothermia confirmed by PM findings in a dependent person at home mandates investigation into possible neglect — a death that appears 'natural' may carry significant medico-legal implications.
